title: The Almoner

where.detail: standing at his cot in the infirmary hall, the almoner on the next cot, Hollis in a carried chair at its foot

time: dawn, the morning after the lid came off
last_beat: Behind them, at the far end of the row, the thin novice was on his knees on the flags with his ear to the floor, listening, and when he saw the Captain looking he got up, and dusted his knees, and went on with his bread.

people.did: Told the thin novice at the night bell and the Prior at the dawn bell, on his own leg with his fingertips wrapped; heard the almoner's confession; stopped Hollis with his full name and an order, the first since the ford; told the almoner to stay in the hall, keep the stores key and give it to nobody.
people.now: Standing at his cot with the ends of his right-hand fingers wrapped in Maelis's linen, the almoner on the next cot under his eye and the stores key still on the man's belt. The next letter from Calden comes up with the carter.

facts.fact: He told the Prior everything in the chapel at the dawn bell, after the far cots' keeper, and said the order of telling was Hollis's asking.
facts.evidence: He told her it had been Hollis's asking that the keepers came first, because it was.

facts.fact: He knows there is a second way down to the undercroft: the old wine stair from the stores, opened by the stores key, which comes out behind a pillar at the kitchen end of the hall below.
facts.evidence: So there were two ways down.

facts.fact: He stopped Hollis with his full name and the voice from the ford, which he had not used since the water, and ordered him to sit.
facts.evidence: It came out of Darrow in the voice from the ford, the one that had put the Ninth into a line it did not want to hold.

facts.fact: He ordered the almoner to stay in the hall, eat, and keep the stores key on him, giving it to nobody, not the Prior, not Darrow himself.
facts.evidence: You'll keep the stores key on you and you'll give it to nobody, not the Prior, not me.

facts.fact: He stood up without remembering getting up, and the knee held.
facts.evidence: He did not remember getting up. The knee held.

people.did: Heard it all in the chapel before the lamps were lit, said once that she had counted the nights between, two, and that she says every name under the roof every night and will go on saying all of them; asked nothing.
people.now: In the chapel at dawn, the first lamp lit. She knows what is under the House and has said her one thing about where she came in the order of telling.

facts.fact: She counted the nights between his promise at the stair head and his telling: two.
facts.evidence: I counted the nights between. Two.

facts.fact: She says every name under the roof in the chapel every night, has not had to stop saying one since he came, and will go on saying all of them.
facts.evidence: I say every name under this roof in this chapel every night, Captain, and I have not had to stop saying one since you came. I shall go on saying all of them.

people.did: Had himself carried in a poled chair at the end of the dawn bell with the almoner walking in front of it, having had the man's confession at the third bell; leaned at him with his whole weight when the man said mercy; stopped at his full name and sat back at the Captain's order.
people.now: In the carried chair at the foot of Darrow's cot, the lad's blanket folded on his knee, his hands off the poles. He said Captain.

facts.fact: He had the almoner's confession at the third bell of the night and brought him to the Captain at dawn.
facts.evidence: Tell the Captain what you told me at the third bell.

facts.fact: He stopped at his full name and the order to sit, and said Captain.
facts.evidence: "Captain," he said.

people.did: Was brought to the Captain shaking, and confessed: the stores key opens the old wine stair down to the undercroft; a clerk in grey at the winch-house, who wrote and never knelt, gave him two wrapped things before the snow and called them a mercy for the wounded, with his sister's letter under his hand; he set the first under the hall by the wine stair and was sick on the stair; the second was still in his satchel, and he gave it to Maelis.
people.now: On the cot next to Darrow's, ordered to stay in the hall where the Captain can see him, to eat, and to keep the stores key and give it to nobody. The next letter from Calden comes with the carter.

facts.fact: The stores key opens the old stair door where the wine was laid, below the kitchen end; the stair comes out in the undercroft hall behind a pillar at the kitchen end; he never used the flour door.
facts.evidence: It comes out in the hall below, at the kitchen end, behind a pillar. I never went near the other door.

facts.fact: A clerk in grey with a desk at the winch-house, older than the grey cloaks and not one of them, gave him two wrapped things before the snow and had his sister's letter, written in the clerk's hand and signed with her private mark.
facts.evidence: He had a desk in the winch-house, they'd put a board on two kegs for him, and he had my sister's letter.

facts.fact: The clerk called the things a mercy for the wounded: the fever comes off a man through the floor if there is a stone to take it, as at the Spire; one under the hall, then the other under the far cots.
facts.evidence: He said the fever comes off a man through the floor if there's a stone to take it

facts.fact: He set the first by the wine stair with a trowel and a lamp and was sick on the stair; he never set the second.
facts.evidence: I set it and I came up and I was sick on the stair.

facts.fact: His sister Mirren went to the Spire at Calden to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, asked the wrong man in front of the wrong people, and is kept at Calden, comfortably, the clerk said twice.
facts.evidence: She went to the Spire to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, because they'd stopped, and she asked the wrong man, in front of the wrong people, and now she's—kept.

facts.fact: He never saw the clerk kneel; the grey cloaks all kneel at the dawn bell, and the clerk only wrote.
facts.evidence: "I never saw him kneel," Anselm said, to the floor.

facts.fact: He says the letters from Calden come up with the carter every seventh day, and there is always another letter.
facts.evidence: They come up with the carter

people.did: Came up behind Hollis's chair unheard, held out her hand for the second wrapped thing, closed her fingers on it, put it in her coat and said nothing more.
people.now: At the cot with the second wrapped thing in her coat beside the chip. She has said nothing to Darrow since the night of the lid but Give it here.

facts.fact: She took the second wrapped thing from the almoner's satchel into her coat without a word about it.
facts.evidence: she closed her fingers on it and looked at nothing, and put it in her coat, and said no more than that

codex.name: The wine stair
codex.text: A second way down to the undercroft: the old stair door where the House's wine was once laid down, below the kitchen end, opened by the almoner's stores key. Its stair comes out in the painted hall behind a pillar at the kitchen end, far from the iron-banded door and its flour. Brother Anselm carried the black sliver down it with a trowel and a lamp (Ch 4 Sc 1).

codex.name: Brother Anselm
codex.text: The House's almoner: a soft, tired lay brother in his forties with ink on two fingers, who keeps the stores and takes the letters down to the carter each week. Before the snow a clerk in grey at the winch-house gave him two wrapped things and called them a mercy for the wounded, with his sister's letter under his hand; he set one under the row by the wine stair and could not set the other. Hollis brought him to the Captain at dawn (Ch 4 Sc 1).

codex.name: Mirren
codex.text: Brother Anselm's sister, the brave one of the two by his account: she went to the Spire at Calden to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, asked the wrong man before the wrong people, and is kept at Calden, comfortably, a clerk said twice. Her letters to her brother come up the cage in the clerk's hand with her private mark under them (Ch 4 Sc 1).

fired.evidence: I counted the nights between. Two.
Brother. Tell the Captain what you told me at the third bell.
I say every name under this roof in this chapel every night, Captain, and I have not had to stop saying one since you came.

now.against: A clerk in grey at the winch-house who never kneels sent two black slivers up in the House's own satchel, and holds the almoner's sister at Calden; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; the grey cloaks have their hand on the cage; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.
now.next: The next letter comes up with the carter.

title: Her Hand

where.detail: inside the wicket by the gate lamp at dusk, with Hollis in his chair, Wren, the almoner and Rae in the kitchen door

time: dusk, the day after the almoner's confession; the cage went down and came up empty
last_beat: Nobody answered him. The snow came in at the wicket and lay on the flags, and the almoner stood with his sister's hair inside his shirt and the stores key in his fist, and waited to be told.

people.did: Met Rae at the wicket; took the letter and knew its hand from the direction on his brother's letters; asked Rae twice where she had seen it and got only that she had; read Marrant's method whole: the lever, never the blade; heard the dealer holds the mare on his name till the thaw.
people.now: Inside the wicket at dusk with his hand open in the snow, having read the shape of Marrant's method; the almoner beside him waiting to be told what a captain does, and Hollis's question unanswered.

facts.fact: He knows the hand on the almoner's letter: the same upright clerk's hand with a long-tailed y that wrote the direction on all three of his brother's letters, and not Aldric's own.
facts.evidence: He had seen it three times on the outside of folded paper, over blue wax, addressed to the Captain of the Ninth

facts.fact: He believes Marrant's whole method is the lever and that he has never needed a blade: the almoner's sister squeezed with a lock of hair.
facts.evidence: He did not need a blade. He had never needed one. The lever was the whole of his method

facts.fact: He asked Rae twice where she had seen the hand and she would not say.
facts.evidence: "I've seen that hand," she said, to the door.

facts.fact: The feeling is coming back into the ends of his right-hand fingers under the linen as a dull red heat; the cold let go of him a little in the night.
facts.evidence: a dull red heat in the ends of the right one's fingers where the feeling was coming back under the linen

people.did: Came up the Steps at dusk with the almoner's letter inside her cloak rather than leave it in the cage overnight; put it in the Captain's hand, not the almoner's; would not say where she had seen the hand; from the kitchen door, told him the dealer took his name and holds the mare on it till the thaw.
people.now: In the kitchen door with a cup, counted in for the night. She has said she has seen that hand, and will not say where.

facts.fact: She carried the almoner's letter up the Steps herself rather than leave it in the cage overnight with the grey cloak's stool in the byre door.
facts.evidence: I'll not leave a thing like that in the cage overnight with that man's stool in the door.

facts.fact: She says she has seen the clerk's hand before, and will not say where.
facts.evidence: "I've seen it." Her shoulders did something under the cloak

facts.fact: The dealer on the Holloway took the Captain's name as surety: worth the mare's keep till the thaw and nothing past it; after the thaw it is coin or she is sold on.
facts.evidence: He said a captain's word was worth the mare's keep till the thaw, and nothing past it

people.did: Opened his sister's letter standing by the gate lamp; a lock of her dark hair fell from it; read it twice and did not weep; said the words are the clerk's and the mark is hers; said the clerk wrote it so that he would finish.
people.now: Inside the wicket with his sister's letter and her hair inside his shirt and the stores key in his fist, waiting to be told what the Captain will do with him.

facts.fact: His sister's letter says she is well kept, that he has a thing to finish, and that when it is finished he may fetch her home from Calden; it carries her private mark.
facts.evidence: She says they have told her I have a thing to finish, and that when it is finished I may come down to Calden and fetch her home.

facts.fact: He says his sister would never say she was well kept: the words are the clerk's, written for her to sign under.
facts.evidence: She'd never in her life say she was *well kept*. That's his word.

facts.fact: A lock of his sister's dark hair, tied with thread, came in the letter.
facts.evidence: A lock of hair. Dark, and tied with thread.

facts.fact: He did not weep; his face shut.
facts.evidence: The man's face had simply shut, like a door with no handle.

people.did: Had himself carried to the gate; asked, since nobody else would, what a captain does with a man who did a terrible thing for love.
people.now: In his chair inside the wicket with the lad's blanket on his knee, his question unanswered.

facts.fact: He asked what a captain does with a man who did a terrible thing for love, and nobody answered.
facts.evidence: What does a captain do with a man who did a terrible thing for love?

people.did: Saw Rae on the Last Hundred through Pell's glass with something held inside her cloak; ran to tell the Captain; caught the lock of hair before it reached the flags and gave it back.
people.now: Inside the wicket at dusk, having caught the lock of hair; she has no count for this.

facts.fact: She caught the lock of hair before it reached the flags.
facts.evidence: Wren caught it before it reached the flags.

codex.name: The letter from Calden
codex.text: A letter for Brother Anselm that Rae Thorne carried up the Steps rather than leave in the cage: addressed in a neat upright clerk's hand with a long-tailed y, the same hand that wrote the direction on the Captain's three letters from his brother. Inside, his sister's words as the clerk wrote them (she is well kept; he has a thing to finish; then he may fetch her home), her private mark under them, and a lock of her dark hair tied with thread (Ch 4 Sc 2).

fired.evidence: He said a captain's word was worth the mare's keep till the thaw, and nothing past it, and he'd hold her that long on it.

quest.name: The List
quest.on_the_page: The Confessors have come for the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's with a list: Darrow first, Hollis second. What stands between them and the hall is Old Mercy, the sanctuary bell: while it rings at dawn and dusk, no blade passes the gate and no name under it is taken down against its will. Marrant has not drawn a blade in a month. He has camped on the lower terrace, kept the cage, and reached into the House by the lever: a clerk in grey who never kneels sent two black slivers up in the House's own letter-satchel, one of them now set in the rock under the row and making the stone grow frost, and holds the almoner's sister at Calden for the second. Banners that are not grey are on the Holloway, a day off.

struggle: What a captain does with a good man who did a terrible thing for love, with the whole House watching him decide. The sliver stays in the wall under forty beds, one with the rock; the lid is off and whoever set it will know. Maelis has walked away from his telling and keeps two pieces of black glass in her coat. His fingertips are numb under the linen. The knee holds a stair at the Mender's count and no more, and the soft season is not over.

now.against: Marrant works the House by the lever, through a clerk's hand and a cage rope: the almoner's sister is held at Calden, and the clerk who never kneels writes her letters; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.
now.next: What a captain does with a man who did a terrible thing for love.

title: One Question

where.detail: at the open wicket in the grey before the dawn bell, Rae gone down into the cloud on the Last Hundred

time: first light, the morning after the letter from Calden
last_beat: At the turn of the Last Hundred she stopped, the way she had stopped twice before, and spoke without looking back. "I'll tell her."

people.did: Waited for Rae at the wicket before the dawn bell; told her all he knows of her is her oxen's names; asked his one question, what she wants, and let the hand on the letter go; answered hers with the mare's name, Thistle, said for the first time since the river.
people.now: At the open wicket at first light, Rae gone down the Steps with the mare's name. He has said Thistle aloud for the first time since the water.

facts.fact: He said the mare's name, Thistle, to Rae at the wicket, the first time he had said it since the river.
facts.evidence: He had not said it since the water. It came out of him rough

facts.fact: He chose not to ask Rae again about the hand on the letter, judging that asking would cost him the one question he had.
facts.evidence: It was the thing she would not give, and asking for it again would only cost him the one he had.

facts.fact: He sent his own name down for the mare because he will not have her stand in a dealer's byre under somebody else's word.
facts.evidence: I'm not having her stand in a dealer's byre under somebody else's word. If it has to be a bad word, it'll be mine.

facts.fact: He knows the Lowmarch's road song about a grey mare of Edgemoor; his men sang it worse than most; it is older than his mare and was true of her anyway.
facts.evidence: It had not been written about his mare; it was older than both of them. It had been true of her anyway.

people.did: Came along the wall at first light with the ox-bell stilled; allowed him one question since it was a new day; told him she is of Coldmere, that her uncle keeps the inn on the tarn where the list was read, that he paid for the cart and the oxen once and she has been paying him back by the load since, and that she wants once to carry a thing up the mountain and see it come down whole; asked why his name went down for the mare, heard it, said Road's the road, and went down saying she would tell her.
people.now: Gone down the Last Hundred into the cloud at first light, with the mare's name. She means to tell the mare.

facts.fact: She is of Coldmere; her uncle keeps the inn on the tarn, across the road from the bell-house, where the Confessors' list was read.
facts.evidence: The inn on the tarn, the one with the bell-house across the road, where they read your list. My uncle keeps it.

facts.fact: Her uncle paid for the cart and the oxen once, and she has been paying him back by the load since; one day she means to pay the last of it, with nobody's hand on the rope but hers.
facts.evidence: He paid for them, once, and I've been paying him back by the load since.

facts.fact: She does not count the people she has brought to the foot of the Steps; Wren counts; she keeps the faces.
facts.evidence: I don't count them; Wren counts. I keep the faces.

facts.fact: She wants, once, to carry a thing up the mountain and see it come down whole.
facts.evidence: I'd like, once, to carry a thing up this mountain and see it come down whole.

facts.fact: Her rule is one question a night, and she allowed the dawn to count as a new one.
facts.evidence: "One question a night," she said. "You know the rule. It's not night, so I'll allow it's a new one."

facts.fact: She has the mare's name from him and went down saying she would tell her.
facts.evidence: "I'll tell her."

facts.fact: Her saying, as she opened the wicket: Road's the road.
facts.evidence: "Road's the road," she said, and opened the wicket.

codex.name: "Road's the road."
codex.text: Rae Thorne, at the wicket at first light, drawing up her hood to go down: her word for a thing that is what it is and will be walked anyway (Ch 4 Between).

codex.name: Thistle
codex.text: At the wicket at first light Darrow said her name to Rae Thorne, the first time he had said it since the river: she carried him into the Wend and never asked the why or the where, and he will not have her stand in a dealer's byre under anyone's word but his own. Rae went down the Steps saying she would tell her (Ch 4 Between).

now.against: Marrant works the House by the lever, through a clerk's hand and a cage rope: the almoner's sister is held at Calden, and the clerk who never kneels writes her letters; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.

title: What Climbed

where.detail: the infirmary hall, at the undercroft door at the dark end; Sister Pell gone back up the row to her tower for the hour bell

time: the grey after the dawn bell, before the first hour bell, the morning after the letter from Calden
last_beat: She was already going, back up the row toward her tower at the pace she had come, and said the last of it to the hall and not to him. "Four strokes. Don't be clever at it."

people.did: Waited at the undercroft door between the dawn bell and the hour bell for Sister Pell; asked her what the bell says at dusk, said it again plain to her face when she lost it in the light, started to ask about her palms and was stopped with Ask the bell; took the three bells and Old Mercy's crack from her, said the four lines of the dusk verse back and stopped on the third; took on a dusk under the tower.
people.now: At the undercroft door at the dark end of the hall, Sister Pell gone up the row to her tower. He has the dusk verse, and owes her a dusk under the tower in the court, saying it with the strokes where she can see his mouth.

facts.fact: He asked Sister Pell what the bell says at dusk, and when she lost his words in the bad light he said them again plain, to her face, without the joke.
facts.evidence: He turned so the window was on his face and said it again, plain, and left off the joke he had been going to put on the end of it

facts.fact: He said the four lines of the dusk verse back to her and stopped on the third, What climbed, we keep.
facts.evidence: got as far as the third line and stopped on it.

facts.fact: He owes Sister Pell a dusk under the tower, in the court, saying the lines with the strokes where she can see his mouth from the window.
facts.evidence: Dusk. Under the tower, in the court, where I can see your mouth from the window. You'll say them with the strokes

facts.fact: He kept his wrapped right hand inside his shirt when she spoke of the bell poured again with its own crack in it.
facts.evidence: Darrow's right hand was inside his shirt, where the linen was. He left it there.

people.did: Came down the row between the dawn bell and the hour bell; read the Captain's mouth and made him say it plain; refused her hands with Ask the bell; told him the House's three bells, the Small that rings once and flat for a far cot, and how Old Mercy cracked in the Quenching's winter and was poured again with the cracked piece in her; knocked the four lines of the dusk verse out on the undercroft door and made him say them back; told him the third line is not his to say; told him to be under the tower at dusk where she can see his mouth from the window, and went up.
people.now: Gone back up the row to her tower for the hour bell. She has given the Captain the dusk verse and expects him under the tower at dusk, in the court, where she can see his mouth from the window.

facts.fact: She hears with her eyes: fifty years under the bells, she reads a speaker's mouth and loses words said sideways or in bad light.
facts.evidence: Fifty years under them, and whatever she heard now she heard with her eyes.

facts.fact: She will not speak of her hands: asked, she said Ask the bell.
facts.evidence: "Ask the bell," she said, without looking up from her hand, and that was the end of that.

facts.fact: The House has three bells: the hour bell, Old Mercy, and the Small, rung once and flat when one of the far cots goes; the Captain has never heard the Small.
facts.evidence: The third's the Small. Once, flat, when one of them goes.

facts.fact: Old Mercy cracked in the Quenching's winter, before any count she keeps, and was broken up and poured again with the cracked piece in the pour, which is why she has the voice she has.
facts.evidence: They broke her up and poured her again with the cracked piece in the pour, and she came out with that voice.

facts.fact: The dusk verse is said to the rope, one line to a stroke, four strokes, by whoever rings Old Mercy at dusk; nobody below hears it, and she has said it every dusk the bell has rung.
facts.evidence: One line to a stroke, four strokes, and nobody below hears them; she's over them.

facts.fact: She gave the Captain the four lines, knocked out on the undercroft door, and told him the third line is not his to say.
facts.evidence: That one's not yours to say.

facts.fact: She told him to be under the tower at dusk, in the court, where she can see his mouth from the window, and not to be clever at it.
facts.evidence: Four strokes. Don't be clever at it.

codex.name: The Small
codex.text: The House's third bell: rung once, flat, when one of the far cots goes, so the House knows without being told. Darrow has never heard it; the Prior has not had a name to stop saying since he came up (Ch 4 Between).

codex.name: The bells of the House
codex.text: Three, by Sister Pell: the hour bell, which tells the day; Old Mercy, the sanctuary bell, which cracked in the Quenching's winter before any count she keeps and was broken up and poured again with the cracked piece in the pour, so that there is no other voice like hers and never will be; and the Small (Ch 4 Between).

codex.name: The dusk verse
codex.text: Said, not sung, to the rope by whoever rings Old Mercy at dusk, one line to each of four strokes; nobody below hears it. *Day's done and the door's shut. / The blade stays below. / What climbed, we keep. / And the bell says so.* Sister Pell knocked it out on the undercroft door for Darrow and told him the third line is not his to say (Ch 4 Between).

codex.name: "Four strokes. Don't be clever at it."
codex.text: Sister Pell to Darrow, going back up to her tower, having given him the dusk verse and a dusk to say it under the tower where she can see his mouth (Ch 4 Between).

now.against: Marrant works the House by the lever, through a clerk's hand and a cage rope: the almoner's sister is held at Calden, and the clerk who never kneels writes her letters; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.

title: The Ramp

where.detail: the kennels below the cloister, sitting in the straw of the run with his back to the boards and a grey hound asleep across his boot

time: the morning after the letter from Calden, after the hour bell; thaw slush on the cloister ramp
last_beat: Darrow looked at the leg across his boot, the laths and the twine, the weight of her, which was more than he had thought. He did not move his foot.

people.did: Went down the kennel ramp with Wren, the borrowed stick under his arm and used once on the slush; told her plainly she did well catching the hair; let himself down into the straw of the run without kneeling, held out his good hand to a grey bitch who bites, and kept it there when she took it in her teeth; she let go, lay down with her splinted leg across his boot and slept; the kennel-master gave him until the grey cloaks are gone.
people.now: Sitting in the straw of the kennel run with a grey hound asleep across his boot and his left hand bitten and bleeding at the thumb; the fingers of the right are still wrapped. The kennel-master has given him until the grey cloaks are gone.

facts.fact: He told Wren plainly that she did well to catch the lock of hair at the gate before it reached the slush.
facts.evidence: "You caught it," he said. "The hair. At the gate.

facts.fact: He lowered himself into the straw by the post with the bad leg out straight, and made sure it was not kneeling.
facts.evidence: It was not kneeling. He made sure of that.

facts.fact: He held out his good hand to the hound and left it there when she bit it.
facts.evidence: every year of the Lances in him said take the hand back, and he left it where it was.

facts.fact: When the hound let go and stood shaking over the bitten hand, his wrapped hand came toward her on its own and he put it back on his knee.
facts.evidence: The other hand, the wrapped one, had come an inch off his knee toward her without being asked, and he put it back.

facts.fact: The hound bit his left hand through the skin at the thumb, and he did not pull it away.
facts.evidence: the meat of the thumb, a hard clamp and a tooth through the skin

facts.fact: The hound lay down with her splinted leg across his boot and slept, and he did not move his foot.
facts.evidence: put the splinted leg across his boot, and laid her head on her own paws, and shut her eyes.

facts.fact: The kennel-master gave him until the grey cloaks are gone: if the hound is eating from somebody's hand by then, she gets the meat.
facts.evidence: If she's eating from somebody's hand by then, I'll find her the meat.

people.did: Came for the Captain at a run with the count of the hound's bites and the kennel-master's plan to put her down before the grey cloaks see; handed him the borrowed stick; on the ramp counted his decent word as a ramp, not a stair, in the room under the one; watched from the gate and counted the bite: four, one of them a knight.
people.now: At the gate of the kennel run with the borrowed stick, having counted the Captain's bitten hand as the hound's fourth.

facts.fact: She counted the grey hound's bites: two lay brothers and the farrier, who says he has never been bitten by anything in his life.
facts.evidence: She's bitten two lay brothers and the farrier, who says he's never been bitten by anything in his life, so that's three bites and one liar.

facts.fact: She brought the Captain to the hound because they have something in common: a splint on a back leg.
facts.evidence: "You've got something in common."

facts.fact: She told him the kennel ramp was built so that a dog with a bad leg could be got up it.
facts.evidence: built, Wren told him, so that a dog with a bad leg could be got up it.

facts.fact: She counted the Captain's decent word on the ramp: a ramp does not count as a stair, but it can go in the room under the one.

time: the small hours of the night after the letter from Calden, the dawn bell owed
last_beat: "That's paid," he said, to the lad, not to Darrow. "Go to sleep, Captain. You've a bell to answer."

people.did: Sat down with Anselm by the brazier, not close, with the House's paper and ink; told him first that he has not stopped seeing the trowel in his hand, and that he gets every word anyway because the other way is the clerk's; gave him the letter and what it is for, three things for the House and one for the sister, where she is kept and a line in her own hand, the only road that goes toward her; named the risk on her and did not soften it; read the letter as it was written and changed nothing; let Anselm's own line stand; said yes to his vow to answer at the bell at Coldmere.
people.now: On his cot in the small hours with the letter written and inside the almoner's shirt, waiting for the carter and the dawn bell. He has told Anselm every word and what it is for, and keeps the width of the gap between their cots.

facts.fact: He sat on his own cot with the gap between them, as he has since the night the lid came off.
facts.evidence: He sat on his own cot with the width of the gap between them, the way he had sat since the night the lid came off

facts.fact: He said he would have told Anselm every word without Hollis's price, because he will not have one more man in the House sent somewhere on a paper he has not read.
facts.evidence: Hollis made it his price, and I'd have done it without him, so hear it as mine. I'll not have one more man in this House sent somewhere on a paper he hasn't read.

facts.fact: He told Anselm he has not stopped seeing the trowel in his hand, and that he knows the shape of being lied to by a paper, having been sent into a river on one.
facts.evidence: I've not stopped seeing the trowel in your hand, and I'll not pretend I have.

facts.fact: He said Anselm gets every word not because he has earned it but because the other way is the clerk's.
facts.evidence: Not because you've earned it. Because the other way is his.

facts.fact: He gave the letter a purpose for the sister, the one he said he cares about: to learn where she is kept, since a clerk who answers a brother's question about her shawl will name the place or lie about it, and either is more than they have.
facts.evidence: For her, one thing, and it's the one I care about. We don't know where she is.

facts.fact: He refused the trade because it would send Anselm down into their hands and get the sister nothing, and said so though he had read no lie in the Confessor.
facts.evidence: The other one, the trade, sends you down the Steps into their hands and gets her nothing. I'll not take it.

facts.fact: He told Anselm plainly that if the letter is caught she pays for it, and that it is a better risk than another month of doing nothing, and that Anselm could refuse it.
facts.evidence: It's a better risk than leaving her where she is and doing nothing, which is what I've done for a month. That's my judgment. You can refuse it.

facts.fact: He read the letter as it was written and changed no word of it, and let the almoner's own last line stand.
facts.evidence: changed not a word, because it was the letter of a frightened man and nothing he could have given him would have been.

facts.fact: He said yes to Anselm's vow to go down to the bell at Coldmere when it is over and ask aloud what was done with his sister.
facts.evidence: "You keep saying that."

people.did: Heard the Captain say he has not stopped seeing the trowel in his hand, and every word of the letter and what it was for; asked what if it is caught and was answered without softening; said his sister would rather be asked after than traded for, and would be angry at him for the stone first; wrote the letter in his own hand and starts, the second set, the hall quiet, what am I to do, where is she, a line in her hand; added a line of his own, Tell her the loop still holds; folded it unsealed inside his shirt against the lock of hair; vowed to go down to the bell at Coldmere when it is done and ask aloud; lay down facing the Captain and did not sleep.
people.now: On his cot with the letter inside his shirt against his sister's hair, awake, the key back on its cord. He has written the false letter knowing every word's purpose, with a brother's questions in it for his sister and one true line, and means to answer at the bell at Coldmere when it is over.

facts.fact: He asked what happens if the letter is caught, and was told his sister pays and that he could refuse.
facts.evidence: "And if it's caught," said Anselm.

facts.fact: He said his sister would rather be asked after than traded for, and would be angry at him for the stone first, and rightly.
facts.evidence: She'd rather be asked after than traded for. She'd be angry at the trade. She'd be angry at me for the stone first, and she'd be right.

facts.fact: He wrote the letter himself, in starts, with the apologies in: the second is set, the hall is quiet, what is he to do, where is she so he can send their mother's shawl, and a line in her own hand.
facts.evidence: Please tell me where she is, so I can send her mother's shawl before the cold. Please let her write me a line herself.

facts.fact: He added one line of his own under his name, Tell her the loop still holds, so that the clerk would read nothing in it and his sister would know he wrote to her and not to him.
facts.evidence: He'll read it and think nothing. She'll read it and know I'm writing to her and not to him.

facts.fact: He folded the letter unsealed, since the carter sees the House's letters sealed at the winch-house now, and put it inside his shirt against the lock of hair.
facts.evidence: the carter would see it sealed at the winch-house, in front of them, the way all the House's letters went down now.

facts.fact: He vowed that when it is done, caught or not, he will go down to the bell at Coldmere where his father was cried and ask aloud on its steps what they did with his sister, the way she would.
facts.evidence: I'm going to stand on the steps and ask what they did with my sister, out loud, with the village there, the way she would.

people.did: Sat awake across the brazier with the lad's hand in his and his eyes on the roof through the whole of it; when the letter was written and inside the almoner's shirt, said to the lad that it was paid, and told the Captain to sleep, since he had a bell to answer.
people.now: In his chair across the brazier with the lad's hand in his. He has heard the Captain give the almoner every word and called the price paid.

facts.fact: He heard the Captain tell the almoner every word of the letter and what it was for, and called the price paid.
facts.evidence: "That's paid," he said, to the lad, not to Darrow.

codex.name: "Tell her the loop still holds."
codex.text: The one line of Brother Anselm's own at the foot of the letter he wrote at the Captain's asking: nothing to the clerk who reads it, and to his sister, who puts a loop in her M so it will hold, the word that her brother is writing to her and not to him (Ch 4 Between).

fired.evidence: "Before a word goes on that," Darrow said, "you'll have all of it. What it says, what it's for, and what it could cost.

struggle: The false letter is written and held: the second set, the hall quiet, in the almoner's own hand with every word's purpose told, and in it a brother's questions for his sister, where she is kept and a line in her hand, and one true line. It goes down with the carter and is read at the winch-house. If it is believed, the Confessor waits and the clerk may name the place; if it is caught, the next letter up comes without her mark. The answer at the dawn bell is owed under the Prior's roof.
inventory: infirmary shirt and breeches; the right fingertips wrapped, the left thumb bound; the borrowed stick he refuses to use; the false letter, folded unsealed inside the almoner's shirt, waiting for the carter

now.against: Marrant has named his price at the bars and been refused in all but words: the almoner's letter waits inside his shirt for the carter, to be read at the winch-house like every letter now; the grey cloaks read everything; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; one grey cloak has gone down the Steps with a horse and not come back; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.
now.next: The dawn bell under the Prior's roof, and the carter, if she is up; a letter that says the second is set and asks where a sister is kept.
